blocks.text: How can we efficiently sort a list of numbers using the power of divide and conquer? Enter merge sort, a classic algorithm that does just that.

blocks.markdown: Merge sort is a classic example of a divide-and-conquer algorithm. It works by recursively dividing the list into smaller sublists until each sublist contains a single element, and then merging those sublists to produce a sorted list. This approach ensures a time complexity of $O(n \log n)$, making it highly efficient for large datasets.

blocks.title: Divide-and-Conquer
blocks.text: Divide-and-conquer is an algorithm design paradigm that involves breaking a problem into smaller subproblems, solving each subproblem independently, and combining their solutions to solve the original problem.

blocks.markdown:
The merge sort algorithm can be broken down into three main steps: 
1. **Divide**: Split the list into two halves.
2. **Conquer**: Recursively sort each half.
3. **Merge**: Combine the sorted halves to produce a single sorted list.

blocks.title: Merge Sort Example
blocks.prompt: Sort the list [38, 27, 43, 3, 9, 82, 10] using merge sort.

steps.text: Divide the list into two halves: [38, 27, 43, 3] and [9, 82, 10].
Divide [43, 3] into [43] and [3], then merge into [3, 43].
Divide [9, 82] into [9] and [82], then merge into [9, 82].

blocks.markdown: Merge sort is stable because it preserves the relative order of equal elements. This is due to the way elements are merged: when two elements are equal, the element from the left sublist is chosen first.

blocks.title: Stability of Merge Sort
blocks.text: Merge sort is a stable sorting algorithm because it maintains the relative order of equal elements during the merge process.

blocks.title: Analyzing Merge Sort Complexity
blocks.prompt: Derive the time complexity of merge sort using its recurrence relation.

steps.text: The recurrence relation for merge sort is $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)$. This represents dividing the list into two halves and merging them.
Using the Master Theorem, we identify $a = 2$, $b = 2$, and $f(n) = O(n)$. Since $f(n) = O(n^c)$ where $c = 1$, $c = \log_b a = 1$.
According to the Master Theorem, when $f(n) = O(n^c)$ and $c = \log_b a$, $T(n) = \Theta(n^c \log n) = \Theta(n \log n)$.

blocks.answer: The time complexity of merge sort is $O(n \log n)$.

points: Merge sort uses a divide-and-conquer strategy to achieve $O(n \log n)$ time complexity.
It is a stable sorting algorithm, preserving the relative order of equal elements.
The space complexity of merge sort is $O(n)$ due to the additional space required for merging.
